decks.title: Production and Costs — Part 1: Production Function and Returns to a Factor
goals: Define the production function, the short run and the long run
Compute total, average and marginal product from a schedule
Explain the three phases of the law of variable proportions
Relate average product and marginal product

slides.heading: Production: Inputs and Output
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how **output** changes when a **variable factor** is added to fixed factors.

visual.alt: Route map of part 1: production function, short run and long run, total, average and marginal product, law of variable proportions
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A firm turns inputs into output. This part explains the technical link between them. We separate the short run from the long run, compute total, average and marginal product from a schedule of an imagined farm, and study how output responds when more workers are added to a fixed amount of land.

slides.heading: The production function
slides.body_md: A **production function** is the technical relationship between the physical inputs used and the **maximum** output they can give. It is written q = f(L, K).

visual.alt: Flow from inputs through the production function to the maximum output
visual.caption: The production function

slides.narration: A production function states how much output can be had from given inputs. It looks only at physical quantities, such as workers, land and seed, and gives the largest output that those inputs can produce with the known technique. For a farm it links the quantity of wheat to the quantities of labour and land.

slides.heading: Short run and long run
slides.body_md: In the **short run** at least one factor is fixed; in the **long run** all factors can be varied.

rows: At least one factor is fixed
Hariyali Farm: 4 hectares cannot be enlarged this season; workers can be added
The farm buys more land and machines over several years

visual.alt: Table comparing the short run, in which at least one factor is fixed, with the long run, in which all factors can be varied, with imagined Hariyali Farm examples
visual.caption: Short run and long run.

slides.narration: The short run is a period in which at least one factor cannot be changed. On Hariyali Farm the land is fixed for the season, so the farm can only change the number of workers. The long run is a period long enough to change every factor, including land and machines. Returns to a factor are studied in the short run.

slides.heading: Hariyali Farm: total product
slides.body_md: **Total product (TP)** is the total output made with a given quantity of the variable factor. Land is fixed at 4 hectares; workers vary.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined total product of Hariyali Farm: 0, 6, 16, 30, 40, 48, 54, 56, 56, 54, 50 quintals for 0 to 10 workers
visual.caption: Imagined Hariyali Farm, 4 hectares fixed.

slides.narration: The imagined Hariyali Farm of Sarangpur has four hectares of land and hires different numbers of workers. With one worker it makes 6 quintals of wheat, with two workers 16, and with ten workers 50. Total product is the whole output at each number of workers.

slides.heading: Average product and marginal product
slides.body_md: **AP = TP ÷ L**, output per worker. **MP = ΔTP ÷ ΔL**, the addition to total product made by one more worker.

visual.alt: Table of total, marginal and average product of Hariyali Farm for 1 to 10 workers with the phase of each
visual.caption: TP, MP = ΔTP ÷ ΔL and AP = TP ÷ L.

slides.narration: Average product is total product divided by the number of workers. Marginal product is the change in total product when one more worker is hired. The table shows both for the farm. The last column names the phase, which we explain shortly. Notice that marginal product rises at first, then falls, and finally becomes negative.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: MP and AP
slides.body_md: Find the marginal and average product of the 5th and 6th workers of Hariyali Farm.
bullets: Step 1 — MP of the 5th worker = 48 − 40 = **8** quintals.
Step 2 — AP of 5 workers = 48 ÷ 5 = **9.6** quintals.
Step 3 — MP of the 6th worker = **6** and AP of 6 workers = **9**.

visual.alt: Worked table: marginal product of the 5th worker 8 and average product of 5 workers 9.6; marginal product of the 6th worker 6 and average product of 6 workers 9
visual.caption: Imagined Hariyali Farm.

slides.narration: To find marginal product, subtract the earlier total from the new total. With five workers the farm makes 48 quintals and with four it makes 40, so the fifth worker adds 8. To find average product, divide total product by the workers: 48 divided by five is 9.6.

slides.heading: Quick check: first phase
slides.body_md: Name the phase for the first three workers.
slides.narration: Look at the marginal product of the first three workers. Is it rising, falling, or negative? The phase is named after what the marginal product does, not after what total product does. Choose the option that matches the behaviour of the marginal product.

slides.heading: Drawing the product curves
slides.body_md: TP rises, flattens at its maximum and then falls. MP rises, falls and cuts the horizontal axis where TP is highest. AP rises and then falls.

slides.heading: The law of variable proportions
slides.body_md: When a variable factor is added to fixed factors, output first rises at an **increasing rate**, then at a **diminishing rate**, and may finally **fall**.

nodes.label: Phase II: marginal product falls, stays positive
Phase III: marginal product negative, total product falls

visual.alt: Flow of the three phases of the law of variable proportions: increasing returns, diminishing returns and negative returns
visual.caption: Law of variable proportions

slides.narration: The law of variable proportions describes what happens when more of one factor is combined with fixed amounts of the others. First the marginal product rises, which is increasing returns. Then it falls but stays positive, which is diminishing returns. In the last phase it turns negative, and total product falls. This is called negative returns.

slides.heading: Phase I: increasing returns
slides.body_md: Marginal product **rises** with each worker. On the farm, workers 1 to 3 add 6, 10, 14 quintals.

visual.alt: Table of phase I of Hariyali Farm, workers 1 to 3: marginal product 6, 10, 14 rises
visual.caption: Phase I: marginal product rises.

slides.narration: In the first phase, each new worker adds more than the one before. The first three workers of the farm add 6, 10, 14 quintals. The fixed land is under-used when few workers are present, and extra workers allow tasks to be divided so that the land is used better.

slides.heading: Phase II: diminishing returns
slides.body_md: Marginal product **falls but stays at or above zero**. Workers 4 to 8 add 10, 8, 6, 2, 0 quintals. TP still rises, until MP is zero.

visual.alt: Table of phase II of Hariyali Farm, workers 4 to 8: marginal product 10, 8, 6, 2, 0 falls but is not negative
visual.caption: Phase II: marginal product falls, stays at or above zero.

slides.narration: In the second phase, marginal product falls but is not yet negative. Workers four to eight add 10, 8, 6, 2, 0 quintals. Total product still rises, or stays the same at the end, because the extra worker adds little. Each worker now has less land to work with than the one before.

slides.heading: Phase III: negative returns
slides.body_md: Marginal product is **negative**, so TP **falls**. The 9th and 10th workers add -2, -4 quintals.

visual.alt: Table of phase III of Hariyali Farm, workers 9 to 10: marginal product -2, -4 is negative and total product falls
visual.caption: Phase III: marginal product negative.

slides.narration: In the third phase, an extra worker reduces output. The ninth worker changes total product by -2 quintals and the tenth by -4. Workers crowd the fixed land and get in one another's way. A producer who has to pay wages would not want to employ workers in this phase.

slides.heading: Quick check: order of the phases
slides.body_md: Arrange the phases as workers are added.
slides.narration: Think about what happens to marginal product as workers are added one by one. It first rises. Then it falls while still positive. Then it reaches zero where total product is highest. Finally it turns negative. Put the four stages in that order.

slides.heading: The three phases on a graph
slides.body_md: Phase I ends where MP is highest. Phase II ends where MP is zero. Phase III has negative MP.

visual.alt: Graph of average product and marginal product of Hariyali Farm against workers, divided into three shaded phases: phase I up to 3 workers where marginal product rises, phase II from 4 to 8 workers where marginal product falls but is not negative, and phase III from 9 workers where marginal product is negative
visual.caption: Imagined Hariyali Farm. Phase I: workers 1 to 3. Phase II: workers 4 to 8. Phase III: workers 9 to 10.

slides.narration: On the graph, the first dashed line marks the end of increasing returns, after 3 workers, where marginal product is highest. The second dashed line marks the end of diminishing returns, at 8 workers, where marginal product is zero and total product is highest. To the right of it, marginal product is below the horizontal axis.

slides.heading: Why the phases occur
slides.body_md: Phases arise because the **fixed factor** is first under-used and later crowded.

nodes.label: Land fully used: each worker has less land

visual.alt: Flow of reasons for the phases: land under-used, division of tasks, land fully used, overcrowding
visual.caption: Reasons for the phases

slides.narration: With few workers the land is under-used, so each new worker makes better use of it and tasks can be divided. When the land is fully used, each new worker has less land than the one before, so marginal product falls. With too many workers they hinder one another, and marginal product becomes negative.

slides.heading: Average product and marginal product together
slides.body_md: While **MP > AP**, AP rises. When **MP = AP**, AP is at its maximum. While **MP < AP**, AP falls.

visual.alt: Table comparing marginal and average product of Hariyali Farm for 2 to 6 workers: average product rises while marginal product is above it, is highest at 4 workers where they are equal, and falls after
visual.caption: Imagined Hariyali Farm.

slides.narration: Compare the two columns. The marginal product of the third worker, 14, is above the average of 10, so the average has risen. At four workers they are equal at 10, which is the highest average. At five workers marginal product 8 is below the average, so the average falls. Marginal product is the cause of the movement of the average.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Meena's bakery
slides.body_md: Meena's bakery has one oven. Find the phases and where AP is highest.
bullets: Step 2 — MP rises up to the 3rd baker: **phase I**. It falls, staying positive, for bakers 4 to 6: **phase II**.
Step 3 — Baker 7 has MP -4: **phase III**. AP is highest, 12, at 4 bakers, where MP = AP.

visual.alt: Table of total, marginal and average product of Meena's bakery for 1 to 7 bakers, with the phase of each; average product is highest at 4 bakers where marginal product equals it
visual.caption: Imagined Meena's bakery, one oven fixed; dozens of loaves per day.

slides.narration: To find the phases, look at the marginal product column. It rises for the first three bakers, so that is the first phase. It then falls but stays positive for bakers four, five and six, which is the second phase. The seventh baker has a negative marginal product, so total product falls. Average product is highest at four bakers, where it equals marginal product.

slides.heading: Quick check: negative marginal product
slides.body_md: True or false: can total product be positive when marginal product is negative?
slides.narration: Marginal product is the change in total product. If it is negative, total product has fallen, but the fall may start from a high level. Think about whether a total can remain above zero after a decrease. Then decide whether the statement is true or false.

slides.heading: Quick check: average product
slides.body_md: Compute the average product of 6 workers.
slides.narration: Look at the total product for six workers in the table. Divide it by the number of workers. Do not use the change in total product, because that gives the marginal product. Enter your answer in quintals.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Technical relation between inputs and maximum output
At least one factor fixed; all factors variable
AP = TP ÷ L; MP = ΔTP ÷ ΔL
MP rises; MP falls but is positive; MP negative
MP above AP: AP rises; equal at the top of AP; below: AP falls

visual.alt: Summary table of part 1: production function, short and long run, TP AP and MP, phases, relation of AP and MP, maximum of TP

slides.narration: To recap. A production function links physical inputs with maximum output. In the short run at least one factor is fixed. Average product is total product divided by workers, and marginal product is the change in total product. Marginal product rises, falls, and then turns negative, giving three phases. It meets average product at the top of the average, and is zero where total product is highest.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define **production function**, **short run** and **long run** in standard words.
Show **MP = ΔTP ÷ ΔL** and **AP = TP ÷ L** with the working.
Name each phase by the behaviour of **marginal product**, with figures.
State that **MP = 0** where **TP is maximum**.
Say that **MP above AP** raises AP, and **MP equals AP** at the top of AP.
slides.narration: Some tips. Define the production function, the short run and the long run precisely. Show the formulas for average and marginal product with every step of the working. Name each phase by what marginal product does, and quote figures. Remember that total product is highest where marginal product is zero, and that marginal product meets average product at the top of the average.

decks.title: Production and Costs — Part 2: Short-Run Costs
goals: Define total fixed, total variable and total cost
Compute marginal, average fixed, average variable and average cost from a schedule
Describe the shapes of the cost curves
Explain where marginal cost cuts the average cost curves

slides.heading: Short-Run Costs
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **fixed** and **variable** costs, and the cost curves of a workshop.

visual.alt: Route map of part 2: fixed and variable cost, total cost, marginal cost, average costs, shapes and relations
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: A firm must pay for its inputs, and these payments are its costs. In this part we separate fixed from variable costs, build total cost, and compute marginal and average costs from the schedule of an imagined chair workshop. We then study the shapes of the curves and how they are related.

slides.heading: Fixed and variable costs
slides.body_md: In the short run, **fixed costs** stay the same at every output; **variable costs** change with output and are zero when nothing is produced.

rows: Does not change with output in the short run
Rent of the shed, salaries of permanent staff
Changes with output; zero at zero output
Wood, glue, wages of casual workers

visual.alt: Table of total fixed cost and total variable cost with imagined examples from the Karwan chair workshop
visual.caption: Fixed and variable costs.

slides.narration: Fixed costs are those that do not change with output in the short run, for example the rent of the shed and the salaries of permanent staff. They have to be paid even when no chair is made. Variable costs change with output, for example wood, glue and the wages of casual workers. They are zero when the workshop produces nothing.

slides.heading: Total cost
slides.body_md: **Total cost = total fixed cost + total variable cost.** Total cost rises with output because variable cost rises.

visual.alt: Flow from total fixed cost plus total variable cost to total cost
visual.caption: TC = TFC + TVC

slides.narration: Total cost is the sum of total fixed cost and total variable cost. Because fixed cost does not change, total cost changes only when variable cost changes. At zero output total cost is equal to the fixed cost. As output grows, total cost grows, and it never falls.

slides.heading: Karwan workshop: the schedule
slides.body_md: The workshop pays Rs 840 a week as fixed cost. Its total variable cost depends on the chairs made.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined weekly total costs of the Karwan workshop for 0 to 8 chairs: total fixed cost 840, total variable cost 0, 700, 1200, 1560, 2000, 2500, 3060, 3710, 4520, total cost 840, 1540, 2040, 2400, 2840, 3340, 3900, 4550, 5360
visual.caption: Imagined Karwan workshop (Rs per week).

slides.narration: The imagined Karwan workshop pays 840 rupees a week as fixed cost, whatever it makes. The total variable cost is zero at zero chairs, 700 rupees for one chair, and 4520 rupees for eight chairs. Adding the two gives total cost, which is 840 rupees even when nothing is produced.

slides.heading: The three total cost curves
slides.body_md: TFC is **horizontal**; TVC **starts at the origin**; TC **starts at TFC** and lies a constant distance above TVC.

slides.narration: The fixed cost curve is a horizontal line. The variable cost curve starts at the origin, since nothing is spent on variable inputs at zero output, and rises. The total cost curve starts at the fixed cost on the vertical axis and is always 840 rupees above the variable cost curve, so the two curves are parallel.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: total and marginal cost
slides.body_md: Find the total cost of 5 and 7 chairs and the marginal cost of the 6th chair.
bullets: Step 3 — MC of the 6th chair = 3900 − 3340 = **560**.

visual.alt: Worked table: total cost of 5 chairs 3340, total cost of 7 chairs 4550, marginal cost of the 6th chair 560
visual.caption: Imagined Karwan workshop.

slides.narration: Total cost is fixed cost plus variable cost. For five chairs it is 840 plus 2500, which is 3340. For seven chairs it is 4550. Marginal cost of the sixth chair is the rise in total cost when output goes from five to six chairs, which is 560 rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: fixed cost curve
slides.body_md: Pick the shape of the total fixed cost curve.
slides.narration: Ask whether total fixed cost changes when output changes. If a cost is the same at every output, its curve has no slope. Choose the option that describes a curve with no slope.

slides.heading: Marginal cost
slides.body_md: **MC = ΔTC ÷ Δq = ΔTVC ÷ Δq**: the addition to total cost from one more unit.

visual.alt: Table of marginal cost of the Karwan workshop: 700, 500, 360, 440, 500, 560, 650, 810 for 1 to 8 chairs, lowest at 3 chairs
visual.caption: Imagined Karwan workshop.

slides.narration: Marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit. It can be found from total cost or from total variable cost, because the fixed part does not change. In the table, it falls from 700 for the first chair to 360 for the third, and then rises to 810 for the eighth chair.

slides.heading: Average costs
slides.body_md: **AFC = TFC ÷ q**, **AVC = TVC ÷ q**, **AC = TC ÷ q = AFC + AVC**.

visual.alt: Table of average fixed, average variable and average cost of the Karwan workshop for 1 to 8 chairs
visual.caption: AFC = TFC ÷ q, AVC = TVC ÷ q, AC = TC ÷ q.

slides.narration: Average costs are costs per chair. Average fixed cost is fixed cost divided by output. Average variable cost is variable cost divided by output. Average cost is total cost divided by output, and it is the sum of the first two. Average fixed cost falls all the way, while average variable cost and average cost first fall and then rise.

slides.heading: Average fixed cost: a rectangular hyperbola
slides.body_md: AFC **falls throughout** but never reaches zero; **AFC × q = TFC** at every output.

visual.alt: Table showing that average fixed cost of the Karwan workshop falls from 840 to 105 while average fixed cost times output is always 840, which is a rectangular hyperbola
visual.caption: Rectangular hyperbola: AFC × q is constant.

slides.narration: The same fixed cost is spread over more chairs, so the cost per chair keeps falling. It never reaches zero, because a positive fixed cost divided by any output is positive. Average fixed cost multiplied by output is always 840 rupees, which is why the curve is called a rectangular hyperbola.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: averages at 6 chairs
slides.body_md: Find AFC, AVC and AC for 6 chairs.

visual.alt: Worked table at 6 chairs: average fixed cost 140, average variable cost 510, average cost 650 found in two ways
visual.caption: Imagined Karwan workshop.

slides.narration: At six chairs, average fixed cost is 840 divided by six, which is 140. Average variable cost is 3060 divided by six, which is 510. Adding them gives average cost of 650. The same figure comes from dividing total cost 3900 by six, so the two methods agree.

slides.heading: Quick check: total cost
slides.body_md: Complete the equation for total cost.
slides.narration: Total cost has two parts. One part does not change with output. Name the other part, the one that changes with output, to complete the equation.

visual.alt: Graph of per-chair costs of the imagined Karwan workshop: average fixed cost falls throughout, while average variable cost, average cost and marginal cost are U-shaped; marginal cost cuts average variable cost at its minimum of 500 rupees at 5 chairs and cuts average cost at its minimum of 650 rupees at 7 chairs
visual.caption: Imagined Karwan workshop. AFC: 840, 420, 280, 210, 168, 140, 120, 105. AVC: 700, 600, 520, 500, 500, 510, 530, 565. AC: 1540, 1020, 800, 710, 668, 650, 650, 670. MC: 700, 500, 360, 440, 500, 560, 650, 810.

slides.narration: On the graph, average fixed cost falls all the way. Average variable cost, average cost and marginal cost fall and then rise, forming a U. Marginal cost cuts average variable cost at its lowest point, 500 rupees, and cuts average cost at its lowest point, 650 rupees. Average cost reaches its lowest point at a larger output.

slides.heading: Marginal cost and average variable cost
slides.body_md: AVC **falls** while MC is **below** it, is lowest where **MC = AVC**, and **rises** while MC is above it.

visual.alt: Table comparing marginal cost with average variable cost of the Karwan workshop for 2 to 6 chairs: average variable cost falls while marginal cost is below it, is unchanged at 5 chairs where marginal cost equals it, and rises after
visual.caption: MC below AVC: AVC falls; MC above AVC: AVC rises.

slides.narration: Compare marginal cost with the earlier average variable cost. For three and four chairs marginal cost is below it, so the average falls. At five chairs marginal cost equals the average of 500, so it is unchanged, and this is the lowest value. Afterwards marginal cost is above the average and pulls it up.

slides.heading: Marginal cost and average cost
slides.body_md: AC **falls** while MC is **below** it, is lowest where **MC = AC**, and **rises** while MC is above it.

visual.alt: Table comparing marginal cost with average cost of the Karwan workshop for 4 to 8 chairs: average cost falls while marginal cost is below it, is unchanged at 7 chairs where marginal cost equals it, and rises after
visual.caption: MC below AC: AC falls; MC above AC: AC rises.

slides.narration: The same rule holds for average cost. Up to six chairs marginal cost is below the earlier average cost, so average cost falls. At seven chairs marginal cost equals 650, so average cost stays at its lowest value. At eight chairs marginal cost is above it and average cost rises. Marginal cost cuts average cost at its minimum.

slides.heading: The gap between AC and AVC
slides.body_md: **AC − AVC = AFC**. The gap **narrows** as output rises, because AFC falls, but it never becomes zero.

visual.alt: Table showing that the gap between average cost and average variable cost equals average fixed cost and narrows from 420 at 2 chairs to 105 at 8 chairs
visual.caption: The gap AC − AVC is AFC, and it narrows.

slides.narration: Average cost minus average variable cost is average fixed cost. At two chairs the gap is 420 rupees, at four chairs it is 210, and at eight chairs it is 105. The two curves therefore come closer as output rises, but they never meet, since average fixed cost is never zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: types of cost
slides.body_md: Match imagined costs with their types.
slides.narration: For each cost, ask whether it has to be paid even when no chair is made. If it does, it is a fixed cost. If it grows with the number of chairs, it is a variable cost. Match each cost to its type.

slides.heading: Why the cost curves are U-shaped
slides.body_md: The U shape is the law of variable proportions seen from the cost side: rising MP lowers cost per unit, falling MP raises it.

visual.alt: Flow from rising marginal product and falling marginal cost to falling marginal product and rising marginal cost, giving a U shape
visual.caption: Why the cost curves are U-shaped

slides.narration: When marginal product of the variable factor rises, each extra unit of output needs less input, so marginal cost falls. When marginal product falls, each extra unit needs more input, so marginal cost rises. The marginal cost curve is therefore U-shaped, and the average costs follow, with average variable cost and average cost also forming a U.

slides.body_md: Gulmohar Bakery has TFC of 360. Find the starred values.

slides.body_md: Compute the average variable cost of 7 chairs.
slides.narration: Average variable cost is variable cost per chair. Read the total variable cost of seven chairs and divide it by seven. Do not include the fixed cost, which belongs to average cost. Give your answer in rupees.

slides.narration: To recap. Total cost is total fixed cost plus total variable cost. Marginal cost is the change in total cost for one more unit. Average fixed cost falls throughout, while average variable cost, average cost and marginal cost are U-shaped. Marginal cost cuts average variable cost and average cost at their lowest points. The gap between average cost and average variable cost is average fixed cost, and it narrows.

bullets: Write **TC = TFC + TVC** and **AC = AFC + AVC** before computing.
Find **MC** as the change in **TC** (or **TVC**) for one more unit.
Draw the curves with **MC cutting AVC and AC at their minimum points**.
Remember that **AFC falls throughout** and **never touches the axis**.
State that the gap **AC − AVC is AFC**.

When you draw the curves, make marginal cost cut the average variable cost and average cost curves at their lowest points. Remember that average fixed cost falls throughout, and that the gap between average cost and average variable cost is average fixed cost.

sections.heading: 1. Production function, short run and long run
sections.body_md:
A **production function** is the technical relationship between the physical quantities of inputs and the **maximum** physical output that can be produced with them: q = f(L, K), where L is labour and K stands for the other factor, such as land or capital.

In the **short run** at least one factor is fixed, so output can be changed only by changing the variable factors. In the **long run** all factors can be varied.

key_terms.definition_md: The technical relationship between inputs used and the maximum output that can be obtained from them.
A period in which at least one factor of production cannot be changed.
A period long enough for all factors of production to be changed.

sections.heading: 2. Total, average and marginal product
sections.body_md:
**Total product (TP)** is the total output at a given quantity of the variable factor. **Average product (AP)** is TP ÷ L. **Marginal product (MP)** is the change in TP when one more unit of the variable factor is used: MP = ΔTP ÷ ΔL.

On the imagined Hariyali Farm (4 hectares fixed) the third worker takes TP from 16 to 30 quintals, so MP is 14, while AP of three workers is 10.

key_terms.definition_md: The total quantity of output produced with a given quantity of the variable factor.
Total product divided by the quantity of the variable factor used: output per unit of the factor.
The change in total product when one more unit of the variable factor is employed.

visual.caption: TP, MP = ΔTP ÷ ΔL and AP = TP ÷ L.

sections.heading: 3. Law of variable proportions
sections.body_md:
When more and more of a variable factor is combined with fixed factors, the marginal product first rises, then falls, and at last becomes negative.

- **Phase I, increasing returns:** MP rises (workers 1 to 3 of the farm).
- **Phase II, diminishing returns:** MP falls but is not negative (workers 4 to 8); TP still rises or stays at its maximum.
- **Phase III, negative returns:** MP is negative and TP falls (workers 9 to 10).

key_terms.definition_md: As more of a variable factor is added to fixed factors, marginal product first rises, then falls and may become negative.
The phase in which the marginal product of the variable factor rises.
The phase in which marginal product falls but remains non-negative.
The phase in which marginal product is negative and total product falls.

sections.heading: 4. Why the phases occur, and AP–MP relation
sections.body_md:
In phase I the fixed factor is under-used and extra workers allow division of work, so MP rises. In phase II the fixed factor is fully used and each worker has less of it. In phase III the fixed factor is crowded.

**AP and MP:** while MP is above AP, AP rises; where MP equals AP, AP is at its maximum; while MP is below AP, AP falls. **TP is at its maximum where MP is zero.** The MP curve cuts the AP curve at the top of the AP curve.

sections.heading: 5. Fixed, variable and total cost
sections.body_md:
In the short run, **total fixed cost (TFC)** does not change with output (rent, salaries of permanent staff) and is paid even at zero output. **Total variable cost (TVC)** changes with output (raw materials, wages of casual labour) and is zero at zero output.

**TC = TFC + TVC.** On a graph, TFC is a horizontal line, TVC starts at the origin and TC starts at TFC and lies Rs 840 above TVC at the imagined Karwan workshop.

key_terms.definition_md: Cost that does not change with the level of output in the short run.
Cost that changes with the level of output and is zero when output is zero.
The sum of total fixed cost and total variable cost at a given output.

sections.heading: 6. Marginal and average costs
sections.body_md:
**Marginal cost:** MC = ΔTC ÷ Δq = ΔTVC ÷ Δq, the addition to total cost from one more unit.

**Average fixed cost:** AFC = TFC ÷ q. **Average variable cost:** AVC = TVC ÷ q. **Average cost:** AC = TC ÷ q = AFC + AVC.

AFC falls throughout and is a rectangular hyperbola; AVC, AC and MC are U-shaped.

sections.heading: 7. Shapes and relations of the cost curves
sections.body_md:
The MC curve cuts the AVC curve and the AC curve at their **minimum points**: an average falls while MC is below it and rises while MC is above it. The AC curve reaches its minimum at a larger output than AVC, since AFC is still falling. The vertical gap between AC and AVC is AFC; it narrows as output rises (Rs 420 at 2 chairs, Rs 105 at 8 chairs) but never becomes zero.

The U shape arises from the law of variable proportions: rising MP lowers cost per unit and falling MP raises it.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Hariyali Farm turns land, workers, seed and water into wheat. The technical relation that gives the largest wheat output for each combination of these inputs is called the

options.text_md: cost function
production function
demand function
budget line

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** production function. A production function links physical inputs with the maximum physical output they can yield. A cost function links output with money cost, a demand function links price with quantity bought, and a budget line shows what a consumer can afford.

questions.stem_md: Hariyali Farm has 4 hectares of land that cannot be enlarged this season, but it can hire as many workers as it likes. Economists describe this period of production as

options.text_md: the long run, because workers can be varied
the long run, because land is fixed
the short run, because all factors can be varied
the short run, because at least one factor is fixed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the short run, because at least one factor is fixed. Because one input, the land, is stuck at its present size, the farm is in the short run. The long run needs every input to be adjustable, so a fixed amount of land rules it out, and varying workers alone does not make the period long.

questions.stem_md: Karwan chair workshop plans five years ahead and can build a bigger shed, buy new machines and hire more staff. This planning period is the

options.text_md: long run, in which all factors are variable
short run, in which all factors are variable
short run, in which all factors are fixed
long run, in which all factors are fixed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** long run, in which all factors are variable. In the long run the firm can change every input, including the size of the plant. No period is one in which all factors are fixed, and the short run always has at least one fixed factor.

questions.stem_md: At Meena's bakery the total product rises from 20 to 36 dozen loaves when the third baker is hired. The 16 dozen loaves is the third baker's

options.text_md: average product
total product
marginal product
fixed product

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** marginal product. Marginal product is the change in total product when one more unit of the variable factor is used. Average product divides total product by the number of workers, and total product is the whole output, so neither is a change.

questions.stem_md: On Hariyali Farm the marginal product of the first three workers is 6, 10, 14 quintals. For these workers the farm is experiencing

options.text_md: diminishing returns, because total product is small
negative returns, because the workers are few
increasing returns to a factor, because marginal product rises
constant returns, because every worker adds output

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** increasing returns to a factor, because marginal product rises. Increasing returns to a factor means that marginal product rises as more of the variable factor is added. Total product still rises under every phase except the last, so a small total says nothing, and negative returns need a negative marginal product.

questions.stem_md: Using the Hariyali Farm schedule of total product of 0, 6, 16, 30, 40, 48, 54, 56, 56, 54, 50 quintals of wheat for 0, 1, 2 … 10 workers, the farm is in the phase of diminishing returns when it employs

options.text_md: 4 to 8 workers
1 to 3 workers
9 to 10 workers
exactly the one worker with the highest average product

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 4 to 8 workers. Diminishing returns are the stretch where marginal product falls but is not yet negative: workers 4 to 8. The first 3 workers have a rising marginal product, and from worker 9 the marginal product is negative.

questions.stem_md: At Hariyali Farm the 9th worker is hired and total product falls from 56 to 54 quintals. This shows

options.text_md: increasing returns, because workers are more numerous
diminishing returns, because marginal product is positive
a fall in the fixed factor, because land shrinks
negative returns, because marginal product is below zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** negative returns, because marginal product is below zero. Total product falls only when marginal product is negative, which is the phase of negative returns. Here the marginal product is -2. Diminishing returns have a positive marginal product, and land is fixed in the short run, so it cannot shrink.

questions.stem_md: On the imagined farm of Nirmala in Dhanpur, the average product of labour rises when a new worker is added. This must mean that the new worker’s

options.text_md: marginal product is zero
marginal product is greater than the existing average product
marginal product is less than the existing average product
total product is at its maximum

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** marginal product is greater than the existing average product. An average rises only when the extra item is above it, as a high mark raises a class average. If the marginal product were lower, the average would fall; if zero, it would fall; and total product keeps rising while the average product is rising.

questions.stem_md: At the point where the average product curve of a firm reaches its highest value, the marginal product

options.text_md: equals the average product
is greater than the average product
is zero
is at its highest value

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** equals the average product. The marginal curve rises through the average curve from above and meets it at the top of the average curve. Before that point marginal product is above average; after it, below. Marginal product is zero much later, where total product peaks, and its own peak comes earlier.

questions.stem_md: The total product curve of Inkwell Press reaches its highest level when the marginal product

options.text_md: is at its maximum
becomes zero
equals average product
is rising fastest

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** becomes zero. Total product stops rising when an extra operator adds nothing, so its peak coincides with zero marginal product. The maximum of marginal product marks only the end of increasing returns, where total product still rises, and equality with average product happens where average product peaks.

questions.stem_md: When the first few workers join Hariyali Farm, marginal product rises. The most suitable reason is that

options.text_md: land becomes more fertile when workers are added
each worker is paid a higher wage
the fixed land is under-used at first and workers can specialise
workers have to share too little land

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the fixed land is under-used at first and workers can specialise. With too few workers the fixed factor is not fully used, and extra hands allow division of tasks and better use of the land. Soil fertility and wages do not explain output, and sharing too little land is the cause of the opposite phase.

questions.stem_md: After the sixth baker joins Meena's bakery, each extra baker adds less to output than the one before. The main reason is that

options.text_md: bakers become lazy as wages rise
flour is not available
the oven grows smaller with time
the fixed oven and space are shared among more and more bakers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the fixed oven and space are shared among more and more bakers. Diminishing returns arise because the variable factor is added to a fixed factor, so each extra unit has less of the fixed factor to work with. Laziness, shortage of flour and a shrinking oven are not part of the law.

questions.stem_md: In Meena's bakery a seventh baker is added and output changes from 60 to 56 dozen loaves. The marginal product of the seventh baker is

options.text_md: 56 dozen loaves, a case of average product
4 dozen loaves, a case of increasing returns
0 dozen loaves, a case of the maximum total product
-4 dozen loaves, a case of negative returns

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** -4 dozen loaves, a case of negative returns. The marginal product is the change in total product, 56 minus 60, which is -4. A negative value means total product has fallen. 56 is the total, not the marginal, and 4 drops the sign.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a fixed cost for the imagined Karwan chair workshop?

options.text_md: The cost of wood for each chair
The wages of casual workers paid by the chair
The monthly rent of the shed
The glue and varnish used on each chair

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The monthly rent of the shed. A fixed cost does not change with output, and rent is paid even when no chair is made. Wood, casual wages and varnish all rise with the number of chairs, so they are variable costs.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a variable cost for the imagined Gulmohar Bakery?

options.text_md: The salary of the permanent head cook
Flour and sugar used for the cakes
The yearly licence fee
The rent of the shop

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Flour and sugar used for the cakes. Variable costs move with output: more cakes need more flour and sugar. The permanent cook’s salary, the licence fee and the rent stay the same whatever the number of cakes baked.

questions.stem_md: On a graph with output of chairs on the horizontal axis and cost in rupees on the vertical axis, the total fixed cost curve of the Karwan workshop is

options.text_md: a horizontal straight line
a line sloping upwards from the origin
a U-shaped curve
a line sloping downwards

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a horizontal straight line. Total fixed cost is the same at every level of output, so its curve is horizontal at a height of Rs 840. A line rising from the origin describes a cost that grows with output, a U shape fits per-unit costs and a falling line fits average fixed cost.

questions.stem_md: The total variable cost curve of the Kesari Jam Works starts from the origin because

options.text_md: fixed costs are zero in the short run
no variable cost is incurred when nothing is produced
marginal cost is zero at the start
average cost is zero at zero output

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** no variable cost is incurred when nothing is produced. Variable costs arise only when inputs are used for production, so they are zero at zero output. Fixed costs still exist in the short run, and marginal and average cost are not defined at zero output in the usual way.

questions.stem_md: On the Karwan workshop graph the total cost curve lies above the total variable cost curve. At every output the vertical gap between them is

options.text_md: the marginal cost at that output
the average variable cost at that output
zero at the origin and growing after it
Rs 840, the total fixed cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Rs 840, the total fixed cost. Total cost is total fixed cost plus total variable cost, so the gap is always the fixed cost, here Rs 840, whatever the output. The two curves are parallel, so the gap does not grow, and it does not shrink to zero.

questions.stem_md: Karwan workshop divides its fixed cost of Rs 840 by the number of chairs made. The resulting average fixed cost curve

options.text_md: falls throughout and is a rectangular hyperbola
first falls and then rises
is a horizontal line
rises throughout

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** falls throughout and is a rectangular hyperbola. Average fixed cost is a constant divided by a growing output, so it keeps falling but never reaches zero, and output multiplied by it is always equal to total fixed cost, which makes a rectangular hyperbola. It does not rise, because the fixed cost does not grow.

questions.stem_md: Marginal cost of a firm is best defined as the

options.text_md: total cost divided by the number of units produced
total variable cost divided by output
change in total cost when one more unit of output is produced
cost incurred even when nothing is produced

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** change in total cost when one more unit of output is produced. Marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit, the change in total cost divided by the change in output. Dividing total cost by output gives average cost, dividing variable cost by output gives average variable cost, and a cost met at zero output is a fixed cost.

questions.stem_md: The marginal cost curve of the imagined Kesari Jam Works cuts its average variable cost curve

options.text_md: at the highest point of the curve
at the point where output is zero
at the lowest point of the average variable cost curve
never; the two curves are parallel

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** at the lowest point of the average variable cost curve. Marginal cost lies below average variable cost while the average falls and above it while the average rises, so it crosses at the lowest point. The curves are not parallel, they intersect, and nothing is produced at zero output so no crossing happens there.

questions.stem_md: At the Karwan workshop the difference between average cost and average variable cost is Rs 420 at 2 chairs and Rs 105 at 8 chairs. This gap is

options.text_md: average fixed cost, which becomes smaller as output rises
marginal cost, which becomes smaller as output rises
total fixed cost, which stays unchanged
average variable cost, which becomes larger as output rises

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** average fixed cost, which becomes smaller as output rises. Average cost is average fixed cost plus average variable cost, so what is left after subtracting the variable part is the average fixed cost. It falls from Rs 420 to Rs 105. Total fixed cost does not change but is not a per-unit figure, and marginal cost is a different concept.

questions.stem_md: The average variable cost curve of a workshop is U-shaped mainly because of

options.text_md: a steady fall of fixed cost with output
a rise in the price of the product
a fall in the number of workers
increasing and then diminishing returns to the variable factor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** increasing and then diminishing returns to the variable factor. When marginal product rises, each unit needs less input, so cost per unit falls; when marginal product falls, cost per unit rises. This is the law of variable proportions seen from the cost side. A falling fixed cost shapes average fixed cost, and the product price has no role in cost curves.

questions.stem_md: At Gulmohar Bakery the average cost of 4 cakes is Rs 245. The fifth cake has a marginal cost of Rs 200, which is below Rs 245. After the fifth cake the average cost will

options.text_md: rise above Rs 245
fall to Rs 236
stay at Rs 245
become Rs 200

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** fall to Rs 236. The extra cake costs less than the average, so the average is pulled down: total cost of 5 cakes is Rs 1,180, and Rs 1,180 divided by 5 is Rs 236. A rise would need a marginal cost above the average, and the new average does not equal the marginal cost.

questions.stem_md: In the Karwan schedule average cost is Rs 650 at 6 chairs and the marginal cost of the 7th chair is Rs 650. What follows for the 7th chair?

options.text_md: Average cost stays at its lowest value, because marginal cost equals average cost
Average cost rises, because marginal cost is above average cost
Average cost falls, because marginal cost is below average cost
Average fixed cost rises, because output has grown

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Average cost stays at its lowest value, because marginal cost equals average cost. The marginal cost of the 7th chair, Rs 650, equals the earlier average, so the average does not move: Rs 4,550 divided by 7 is Rs 650, the same as before. Marginal cost is neither above nor below it, and average fixed cost always falls with output.
